q: You are two days out on an offshore passage, where the boat is drawn, south of the centre of this high. Where does the wind come from?
a: From about ENE
o: From about WSW
From about ESE
From about N
why: Round a high in the north air turns clockwise and slightly outwards: on its south side it blows from about ENE.
ref: Pressure systems — wind round a high

o: S 3–4, backing SE by the afternoon
Light and variable under the high
W 5–6 onshore, a sea breeze by noon
why: High to the NW, heat low over Iberia: the summer northerly (nortada) — strongest in the afternoon and off the capes.
ref: Pressure systems — Azores high and the heat low

a: Light, variable wind, with fog or thunder
o: A steady fresh breeze from the nearest high
A gale from the deeper of the two lows
Clear skies and a steady sea breeze
why: A col between two highs and two lows has slack, shifting winds; in warm moist summer air it brings fog or thunderstorms.

q: You are deciding whether to start a 3-day passage south across Biscay, and the forecaster's notes mention the jet stream. What does it tell you?
a: Lows will run fast along it, one after another
o: Gales at the surface wherever the jet blows
A blocking high will hold for the whole week
Nothing — it is too high to affect the sea
why: A strong straight jet steers and feeds surface lows: they form, deepen and race along beneath it in a quick series.
ref: Depressions — the jet stream as context

q: You are in port at 50°N with a two-day passage planned, and you compare two analysis charts 24 hours apart. What is this low doing?
a: Deepening explosively — storm force near it
o: Filling slowly — the worst of it is over
Deepening normally — a gale at most
Moving away — the fall is only diurnal
why: 28 hPa in 24 h is past the bomb rate (about 21 hPa at 50°N): an explosive low — storm-force winds round it are likely.
ref: Depressions — explosive deepening

q: You are one day out on a passage south-west of Ireland and read the latest analysis. Where do you watch for a new low that could reach you?
a: At the triple point, where the fronts meet
o: Over Iceland, where the old low re-deepens
Behind the cold front, in the polar air
Along the warm front, far to the east
why: A new (secondary) low often forms at the triple point of an old occluded system — here 150 M from your route.
ref: Depressions — occlusion and the triple point

a: A stationary front — long rain, poor visibility
o: An occlusion — one sharp veer, then clear
A cold front — a squall line, then clear
A trough — showers, then a ridge behind
why: Triangles and semicircles on opposite sides mark a stationary front: wide cloud, long spells of rain and poor visibility.

q: You are on passage in the warm sector, and you get this at 1000 UTC. At about what time does the front reach you if you hold your course?
a: About 1546 UTC
o: About 1730 UTC
About 2043 UTC
About 1617 UTC
why: Closing speed 20 + 6 = 26 kn: 150 ÷ 26 = 5.77 h = 5 h 46 min after 1000 — about 1546 UTC.
ref: Fronts — timing the cold front

fig.title: Analysis received 1000 UTC
lines: Cold front 150 M W of you

q: You are 120 M offshore when the cold front goes through and the wind veers sharply from SW to NW. What sea do you meet for the next few hours?
a: A confused cross sea — old SW on new NW
o: A smooth sea — the new wind flattens the old
A long, regular swell from the NW only
The same SW sea, simply easing at once
why: After a big veer the old SW sea keeps running while the NW wind raises a new one across it: a confused, breaking cross sea.
ref: Fronts — the sea after a veer

q: You are planning which side of an approaching low's track to be on during the passage. Which of the two yachts meets the stronger wind?
a: B — the low's motion adds to its wind there
o: A — the low's motion adds to its wind there
Both the same — they are equally far off
A — it lies closer to the colder air
why: On the right of a moving low's track (NH) the wind blows the way the low travels, so the two add: SE of a NE-bound low.
ref: Depressions — the stronger side of the track

a: A rapidly deepening low
o: A dying low — its cloud breaking up
A ridge, with clearing air behind it
A heat low over the warm sea
why: A comma-shaped cloud head with a dry slot cutting in and cooling tops is the signature of a low deepening fast.

o: As a dying storm — it will be weak by then
As a tropical storm — only its eye is a risk
As no risk — such storms never reach here
why: Ex-hurricanes often re-deepen as ordinary lows on reaching cooler water and can bring severe gales to European waters.

o: About 50 kn
About 12 kn
About 17 kn

a: B, round the high
o: A, round the deep low
Both alike — the scale holds
Neither — the scale is the gust
why: Gradient wind: curving round a low the wind is less than geostrophic, round a high it is more, for the same spacing.

About 31 kn from 255° — F7

a: 0000 UTC Tuesday
o: 0430 UTC Tuesday
1200 UTC Monday
1200 UTC Tuesday

ref: Synoptic charts — prognosis valid time

a: About 26 kn — F6
o: About 34 kn — F8
About 30 kn — F7
About 15 kn — F4

a: Force 8 — gale
o: Force 6 — strong breeze
Force 7 — near gale
Force 10 — storm

a: 48–55 kn, waves of 6 to 9 m
o: 41–47 kn, waves of 4 to 6 m
56–63 kn, waves of 9 to 14 m
48–55 kn, waves of 4 to 6 m
why: Storm 10 is a mean of 48–55 kn; sea state 'high' is 6–9 m (very rough 4–6, very high 9–14).
ref: Storm warnings and sea-state terms

a: About 6.5 m
o: About 3.5 m
About 4.4 m
About 2.2 m
why: 3 h of 8-s waves is about 1350 waves, so the 1-in-1000 wave will come: 1.86 × 3.5 = 6.5 m.
ref: Sea state — significant and maximum wave height

q: You must decide whether to carry on through the night in this new wind. What significant height do you plan for, and what odd wave?
a: Hs 3.3 m, the odd one near 6 m
o: Hs 3.6 m, the odd one near 6.7 m
Hs 4.6 m, the odd one near 8.6 m
Hs 3.3 m, the odd one near 3.3 m
why: The sea is limited by the smaller of fetch and duration: 100 M gives 3.3 m; 1.86 × 3.3 ≈ 6 m for the biggest of the night.
ref: Sea state — fetch and duration tables

a: About 1600 Tuesday
o: About 2000 Monday
About 1200 Wednesday
About 0800 Thursday
why: Wave speed 3 × 15 = 45 kn; the swell's energy travels at half, 22.5 kn: 900 M takes 40 h — Monday 0000 + 40 h.
ref: Sea state — swell travel

a: A — short and steep, its crests break
o: B — the higher sea is always worse
B — its long period hits harder
Neither — 5 m is fine for 14 m
why: Steepness, not height, makes crests break: 4 m in 6 s (about 56 m long) is steep; 5 m in 13 s (260 m) is a long, safe swell.

o: At A — in the deep ocean
At C — on the shelf, nearer land

Little — so plan on the average, W 5

The S route — it is shorter in miles

o: The global GRIB — it covers the whole route
The global GRIB — its wind is the lighter
The average of the two — about 18 kn
why: A 25 km grid smooths the mountains away; a 2 km model resolves the gap winds where the harbour lies.

q: You are 100 M offshore in the western Approaches in June. Which fog do you expect out here?
a: Advection fog — moist air cooled by the sea
o: Radiation fog — the sea cools at night
Frontal fog — rain into cold air
Sea smoke — cold air over warm sea
why: Far out at sea the water hardly cools at night: fog there is advection fog, warm moist air cooled from below by colder sea.
ref: Fog — types at sea

q: You are closing the Portuguese coast after a night offshore in the August northerly. Where do you expect to meet fog?
a: Inshore, over the cold upwelled water
o: Offshore, over the warmer water
Nowhere — a fresh N wind keeps fog away
Only after dark, as the land cools
why: The northerly lifts cold water along the coast: the sea inshore is below the 16°C dew point, the sea offshore is above it.
ref: Fog — coastal upwelling

q: You plan to cross the shipping lanes over the shelf tonight. Do you expect fog over the shelf?
a: Yes — dew point about 15°C, above the 14°C sea
o: No — dew point about 3°C, far below the sea
No — dew point about 1°C, far below the sea
No — the air is 4°C warmer than the sea
why: 18 − (100 − 85)/5 = 15°C dew point: air cooled over 14°C water passes its dew point — fog is likely.
ref: Fog — predicting it from the dew point

q: You are leaving a Norwegian fjord at dawn in January. What do you see over the water?
a: Sea smoke — steam off the warmer sea
o: Advection fog — moist air over cold sea
Radiation fog — drifting off the land
Haze — salt from the breaking waves
why: Very cold air flowing over much warmer water makes steam fog (sea smoke), thickest near the shore the air comes from.
ref: Fog — sea smoke

q: You are making your landfall along this straight coast at the end of a two-day passage. What wind do you expect in the last 10 M close along it?
a: More wind — convergence along the coast
o: Less wind — the land shelters you
The same — the coast is straight
Less wind — divergence along the coast
why: NH: wind blowing along a coast with the land on its right, looking downwind, converges there and blows harder than offshore.
ref: Local effects — coastal convergence

o: A — on the windward face, in the full trade
C — close under the lee, out of the trade
D — well out in the lee, in clear air
why: A high island under the trade inversion turns the wind round its ends: acceleration zones off the flanks, a wind shadow in the lee.

o: 0.5 M off — the cliffs give a lee
0.5 M off — the shortest way in
3 M off — the swell is smaller there
why: Swell reflected off cliffs crosses the incoming waves within a mile or so: a steep, confused sea. Keep a few miles off.

A sudden shift to E, gusts of 20 kn

About 1442
About 1342

o: Turn west to meet it and pass behind it
Stop and let it pass ahead of you
Turn east and run ahead of it

a: In the oven — the metal box screens them
o: In a dry bag in the cockpit locker
On the chart table, switched on
In the bilge, out of the way
why: A closed metal box like the oven acts as a Faraday cage and may save the spare electronics from a strike.

q: You plan an overnight crossing of the western Mediterranean in September. When are the thunderstorms most likely on your crossing?

o: Mid-afternoon, as they are over land
At sunset only, as the air cools
Never at sea — only over the hills
why: Over a warm sea, storms peak at night and early morning, when cold air aloft makes the air most unstable; over land, by afternoon.

In neither — both means under 30 kn

lines: Low 990 hPa moving NE at 25 kn

q: You are hove-to in mid-Biscay at night as this low tracks east right over you. What do you prepare for next?
a: A NW gale, coming in within an hour or two
o: A slow veer to S, then SW, easing
Calm until dawn, as the low fills
The SE gale again, from the same side
why: When a centre passes right over you the wind dies at the lowest pressure, then comes back hard from the opposite side — here the NW.
ref: Depressions — the centre passing over you

fig.title: Night log, mid-Biscay
lines: Forecast: centre tracking E over you

q: You are on day two of a Biscay crossing and read back today's log. What has passed over you?
a: An occlusion — the warm sector never reached you
o: A warm front — the cold front is still to come
A cold front — the warm one passed in the night
A trough — the low's fronts are still to come
why: One band of rain, a single veer and no warm, damp spell: the cold front has lifted the warm sector off the sea — an occlusion.
ref: Fronts — the occlusion

fig.title: Day log, mid-Biscay
lines: No warm, muggy spell all day

q: You are 100 M out on a passage south-west when the weather turns back on you after the cold front. What is happening?
a: A wave low is running NE along the front
o: A heavy shower — the NW will be back soon
The warm front again — clear skies behind
The old low filling — the rain will fade
why: The front has stalled and a wave is forming on it: a secondary low runs along the front, the wind backs, rain returns, and it may deepen.
ref: Depressions — a wave on the cold front

fig.title: Log after the cold front
lines: Chart: a wave on the front 200 M SW

q: You read this analysis, with a secondary low south of the main one, before choosing your track. At which point do you expect the strongest wind?
a: B — on the far side of the secondary
o: A — between the two centres
C — at the secondary's centre
D — at the main low's centre
why: On the side of a secondary away from the main low the two circulations add: the strongest wind. Between the two centres they oppose.
ref: Depressions — the secondary low

q: You are planning a three-day passage from Lisbon to Madeira, and the forecaster's notes say this. How do you treat the low in your plan?
a: Slow and erratic — low confidence, keep updating
o: Fast — the jet will sweep it NE within a day
Gone — it will fill before you sail
Harmless — the jet will steer it W, away
why: Cut off from the jet, a low is no longer steered: it drifts slowly and erratically, the models disagree, and it can sit for days.
ref: Depressions — the cut-off low and the jet

fig.title: Forecaster's notes, Thursday
lines: Jet stream buckled into a deep loop
A low has cut off W of Portugal
The models disagree on its track

q: You are planning a two-day passage north along the Norwegian coast in January, and this is in the forecaster's notes. What does it warn you of?
a: Small, fierce lows — gales at short notice
o: Large, slow lows — days of warning first
Clear, settled cold — the best of sailing
Thick fog — light winds for days
why: Polar lows form fast in Arctic air over a warmer sea: small and intense, often missed by the models — gales and snow with little warning.
ref: Depressions — the polar low

fig.title: Forecaster's notes, January
lines: Your passage: 2 days N along the coast

q: You plan to cross the Ionian from Sicily to Greece late in October, and this is in the forecast notes. What do you decide?
a: Postpone — a small, intense storm may form
o: Go — it will bring only heavy rain
Go — such storms happen only in the tropics
Go — it will give you a fair NW breeze
why: A medicane is a small, tropical-like Mediterranean cyclone over a warm autumn sea: storm-force winds, and a track poorly forecast.
ref: Depressions — the medicane

fig.title: Forecast notes, Tuesday
lines: Sea 25°C, cold air aloft over Sicily
No port of refuge on the way

q: You are bound for the Faroes at 60°N, and your chart's geostrophic scale was made for 40°N. What wind does the isobar spacing over you give?
a: About 22 kn — F6
o: About 41 kn — F9
About 30 kn — F7
About 20 kn — F5
why: Geostrophic wind goes as 1 / sin(latitude): 30 × 0.64 ÷ 0.87 = 22 kn. The same spacing gives less wind at a higher latitude.
ref: Surface analysis — the geostrophic scale with latitude

fig.title: Geostrophic scale on the chart
lines: Spacing over you reads 30 kn on it

q: You measure the gap between two isobars along 50°N on a small-scale chart, in degrees of longitude. What geostrophic wind do you get?
a: About 39 kn — F8
o: About 25 kn — F6
About 32 kn — F7
About 16 kn — F4
why: 2° of longitude at 50°N is 120 × cos 50° = 77 M, not 120 M: 3000 ÷ 77 = 39 kn. Distance is never measured on the longitude scale.
ref: Surface analysis — measuring the isobar spacing

q: You are reading the general synopsis of a high seas bulletin before leaving Falmouth for Spain. What does it say the low will do?
a: Move to Fastnet and deepen by 12 hPa
o: Move to Fastnet and fill by 12 hPa
Stay where it is and deepen to 970
Die out, as a new 970 low forms at Fastnet
why: 'Expected Fastnet 970 by 0000' gives where the centre will be and its pressure then: 982 to 970 hPa is a deepening of 12 hPa.
ref: Forecast products — the high seas synopsis

q: You are bound south-west, and this is your area forecast in the high seas bulletin. Will the change head you?
a: Yes — it backs to SW, onto the nose
o: No — it veers to SW, onto the beam
No — 'backing' means it is easing
Yes — it veers to SW, onto the nose
why: Backing is an anticlockwise shift: NW to SW is a back of 90°, and a SW wind is dead ahead on a course of SW.
ref: Forecast products — high seas wording

q: The high seas bulletin gives this for the area next to yours, and your crew is alarmed by the word. What does it mean?
a: Force 12: a mean of 64 kn or more
o: A true hurricane, eye and all
Gusts to 64 kn round a force 10 mean
An ex-hurricane that keeps its eye
why: 'Hurricane force' is simply Beaufort 12 — a mean of 64 kn or more — and is used for deep mid-latitude storms too.
ref: Forecast products — Beaufort terms in a bulletin

q: You plan to cross Biscay in two days, and the synopsis says this about the low there now. What will it do?
a: Fade out — no longer a low of its own
o: Deepen fast — too quick to track
Leave the bulletin's area to the E
Join the next low as a gale centre
why: 'Losing its identity' means the low is dying out or merging into the general pattern: it will no longer be a separate centre.
ref: Forecast products — the synopsis wording

q: You are in mid-passage, out of NAVTEX and VHF range, with no satellite terminal aboard. How do you get the surface analysis and the prognoses?
a: By HF weatherfax, decoded on the laptop
o: From NAVTEX, set to a distant station
On VHF Ch 16, from the coastguard
From the GRIB saved before you left
why: An SSB (HF) receiver picks up radiofax broadcasts of analysis and prognosis charts thousands of miles away; a laptop decodes them.
ref: Forecast products — HF radiofax

fig.title: Mid-passage, day 2
lines: 300 M from NAVTEX and VHF stations

q: You are ordering a GRIB by satellite phone for the next three days of your passage. Which request do you send?
a: Your route only, 0.5° grid, 3-hourly, wind and pressure
o: The whole North Atlantic, 0.25°, hourly, every layer
Your route only, but with every layer on offer
The whole ocean at 2°, wind only, 24-hourly
why: On a slow, paid link ask only for what you need: a small box, wind and pressure, 3-hourly — a small file that is still useful.
ref: Forecast products — ordering a GRIB at sea

q: You download a GRIB at 1000 UTC on the morning you sail. Which model run do you get, and how old is it?
a: The 0000 UTC run — already 10 h old
o: The 0600 UTC run — 4 h old
The 1200 UTC run — just out
The 1800 UTC run — 16 h old
why: The 0600 run is not ready until 1030, so at 1000 the newest is the 0000 run: its data are already 10 h old.
ref: Forecast products — GRIB model runs

fig.title: Global model
lines: Each is ready about 4½ h after

q: You must decide whether to leave on a 30-hour crossing, and your three sources disagree. Do you go?
a: No — the bulletin and the ensemble both flag a gale
o: Yes — the GRIB shows only 18 kn all the way
Yes — a 35 % chance means it probably won't come
Yes — and steer round the gale using the GRIB
why: One model run shows no gale, but a 1-in-3 ensemble chance and the forecaster's 'gale 8 later' say it may come: no-go for a 30-h leg.
ref: Forecast products — GRIB, ensemble and the official forecast

fig.title: Go/no-go, 30-h crossing
lines: GRIB, one model run: SW 18 kn
Ensemble: 35 % chance of a gale, day 2
No port of refuge on the way

q: You are choosing between two routes for a two-day passage from this ensemble output. Which do you take?
a: The S route — it cuts the risk to 20 %
o: The rhumb line — it saves 9 hours
The rhumb line — 70 % is not a certainty
The S route — there the chance is nil
why: Seven in ten members give force 7 or more on the rhumb line; nine more hours at sea for a one-in-five risk is the better bet.
ref: Forecast products — the ensemble for routeing

fig.title: Ensemble, day 2 of your passage
lines: Chance of a mean force 7 or more:
S route: 9 h longer at sea

q: Your routing software gives this ETA for a 210-mile passage. When do you really expect to arrive, against the front?
a: In about 37½ h — 3½ h after the front
o: In about 36 h — 2 h after the front
In about 24 h — 10 h before the front
In about 30 h — 4 h before the front
why: At 80 % of the polars the passage takes 30 ÷ 0.8 = 37½ h — after the front. Multiplying by 0.8 or adding 20 % is the slip.
ref: Weather routing — the polars

fig.title: Weather routing, 210 M
lines: Router ETA: 30 h, at 100 % of polars
Cold front at the destination: in 34 h

q: You download a satellite wind pass at sea and compare it with the GRIB for the same hour. Which do you plan the next 12 hours on?
a: The satellite pass — it measured the wind
o: The GRIB — it covers the next 12 hours
The GRIB — satellites cannot see wind
The average of the two — about 30 kn
why: A scatterometer pass (ASCAT) measures the surface wind from the sea's roughness; when it shows more than the model, the model is low.
ref: Forecast products — satellite winds and the GRIB

fig.title: Your area, 0945 UTC
lines: ASCAT pass: 35 kn in a band 60 M wide
You: on the band's S edge

q: You are 130 M out on the first night of a passage, and the weather is not what was forecast. What do you make of it?
a: The low is deeper or nearer — reef and replan
o: The barometer is faulty — sail to the forecast
Just a local squall — it will settle back
The forecast is right — the wind is a gust
why: Two forces more and the glass falling fast: your own observations beat an old forecast. Assume the low is deeper or closer than shown.
ref: Forecasts — your own observations

q: You look at the extra layers of tonight's GRIB for your route. What do they tell you?
a: Thunderstorms are likely over the E half
o: A strong, steady wind over the E half
Fog over the E half — the air is saturated
Nothing — CAPE matters only to pilots
why: CAPE is the energy available to rising air: over about 1000 J/kg the air is unstable enough for big Cb — squalls and lightning.
ref: Forecast products — CAPE in a GRIB

fig.title: GRIB layers, tonight
lines: Wind: W 12–15 kn all along the route
CAPE: 1800 J/kg over the E half

q: You are running in from the deep ocean towards the continental shelf with this swell. At about what depth does it start to feel the bottom and steepen?
a: About 153 m
o: About 306 m
About 11 m
About 22 m
why: Deep-water wavelength 1.56 × 14² = 306 m; a wave feels the bottom at half that, about 153 m — just inside the 200 m shelf edge.
ref: Sea state — the shelf and the deep sea

fig.title: Swell from the W
lines: A wave feels the bottom where
the depth is under half its wavelength

q: It is 2200, and you will reach your next waypoint, far out in Biscay, at 1000 tomorrow. What significant height do you plan for there?
a: About 6.3 m
o: About 5.1 m
About 3.4 m
About 8.3 m
why: By 1000 the wind will have blown for 18 h: 6.3 m. The 500 M fetch would allow 8.3 m, so duration limits it; counting from now gives 5.1 m.
ref: Sea state — fetch and duration

fig.title: Wind W 8 (40 kn) since 1600
lines: Hs by duration: 6 h 3.4 m · 12 h 5.1 m
18 h 6.3 m · by fetch, 500 M: 8.3 m

q: You are bound north tomorrow under this forecast. From where do the big waves come?
a: From the W, on your beam
o: From the NE, on the bow
From the E, on the beam
From the SW, on the quarter
why: Swell runs on from the storm that made it, whatever the local wind: here the 4 m comes from the W, on the beam of a northbound yacht.
ref: Sea state — swell and wind sea

q: Your anemometer failed overnight, 100 M offshore, and you log the wind from the sea at 1600. What force do you write?
a: Force 6 — strong breeze
o: Force 5 — fresh breeze
Force 7 — near gale
Force 8 — gale
why: Large waves forming, white foam crests everywhere and some spray: Beaufort force 6, with waves of about 3 m in the open sea.
ref: Beaufort scale — the sea at force 6

fig.title: Log at 1600, anemometer out
lines: Foam not yet blown in streaks

q: You are crossing the Gulf Stream on a passage from Charleston to Bermuda. When do you cross it?
a: Today, before the northerly sets in
o: Tomorrow, on the fresh fair northerly
Tomorrow night, once the N is steady
Any time — the current flattens the sea
why: A northerly against a 3–4 kn NE-going stream raises steep, breaking seas: cross while the wind still runs with the current.
ref: Sea state — wind against an ocean current

fig.title: Gulf Stream crossing
lines: Tomorrow: N 6–7 behind a cold front
Crossing the stream takes about 10 h

q: You skipper a 22 m motor yacht on a 120-mile run into the sea. Which part of this forecast sets your go or no-go?
a: The sea — its height and period ahead
o: The wind force — as for a sailing yacht
The visibility — the radar needs it
The pressure — and how fast it rises
why: Under power the wind itself matters little; the head sea's height and steepness decide how fast — and how safely — she can go.
ref: Sea state — a motor yacht's limits

fig.title: Forecast for the run
lines: Swell NW 3 m, 7 s, after a gale

q: You are skipper of a 22 m planing motor yacht leaving at 0700 for a 132-mile run, and the forecast sea builds from halfway. When do you plan to arrive?
a: About 1600
o: About 1500
About 1900
About 1300
why: 66 M at 22 kn = 3 h, then 66 M at 11 kn = 6 h: 9 h, in at 1600. Averaging the two speeds (16.5 kn) gives 1500 — the slip.
ref: Sea state — a planing yacht slowed by the sea

fig.title: Motor yacht, head sea
lines: Sea over 2 m from halfway on
In over 2 m you slow to 11 kn

q: You skipper a 24 m motor yacht heading into the sea, and four forecasts are possible for tomorrow. Which gives the worst pitching and slamming?
a: Period 4 s
o: Period 12 s
Period 9 s
Period 6 s
why: 1.56 × 4² = 25 m: a wavelength about her own length makes her pitch hardest. 6 s gives 56 m, 9 s 126 m, 12 s 225 m.
ref: Sea state — wavelength and a motor yacht

fig.title: Head sea, Hs 1.5 m in each case

q: You and a friend cross the same beam swell — you in a 22 m motor yacht whose stabilisers have failed, he in a 15 m sailing yacht under main. Why does he roll far less?
a: The wind in his sail damps the roll
o: His keel is heavier than your hull
A shorter boat always rolls less
The swell is smaller where he is
why: Wind pressure on a set sail resists every roll; a motor yacht has no such damping, so a beam swell throws her about.
ref: Sea state — a motor yacht in a beam sea

fig.title: Beam swell, open sea
lines: Swell 2.5 m, 9 s, on the beam

q: You are making a night landfall in thick fog after two nights at sea. Where, and how, do you go in?
a: On to B, in on radar and plotter at slow speed
o: Into A on the plotter, at slow speed
Stand off and wait 24 h for it to clear
Stop off A and wait there for daylight
why: Sea fog will not clear soon; a narrow rocky entrance in fog with a tired crew is the real risk. A wide, deep, buoyed one is the safe landfall.
ref: Fog — a landfall decision

fig.title: Landfall, 0200
lines: Advection fog, forecast to last 24 h+
Port A: 3 M, rocky entrance 1 cable wide
Port B: 15 M on, wide, deep, buoyed
Radar, AIS, GPS fine; crew tired

q: You are approaching the Channel at night in the fog of a warm sector. When do you plan to make your landfall?
a: After 0600, in the clear air behind the front
o: Before 0600, while the wind is still light
At dawn — the sun will burn the fog off
Now — the fog lifts as the wind rises
why: Warm-sector sea fog lasts as long as the warm, moist air: it clears when the cold front brings in the dry polar air.
ref: Fog — clearing behind a cold front

fig.title: Night approach, 2300
lines: Behind it: dry polar air, clear

q: You are closing Gran Canaria after a three-day passage, and the visibility is going. What is cutting it, and how long will it last?
a: Saharan dust — until the wind leaves the east
o: Sea fog — until the sun burns it off
Radiation fog — until mid-morning
Rain haze — until the front passes
why: An east wind off the Sahara carries dust (the calima) out over the Canaries: a dry, yellow haze that lasts as long as the easterly.
ref: Local effects — the calima

fig.title: Canaries landfall, February
lines: Wind E 5, hot and dry, off Africa

q: You are making your landfall to anchor at A, tucked in east of the point, out of this swell. Will A be quiet?
a: No — the swell bends round the point into A
o: Yes — A faces away from the swell
Yes — swell runs only with the wind, now E
No — the light E wind raises a big sea at A
why: Swell refracts as it feels the bottom and wraps round a point into the bay behind it — smaller, but still rolling, a long swell most of all.
ref: Local effects — swell round a point

fig.note: Swell W 3 m, 12 s · wind E 2

q: You are heading east at 6 kn at night, and the radar shows this cell crossing ahead of you. What do you do?
a: Slow down, let it cross, pass astern of it
o: Speed up and cross ahead of it
Turn N to meet it and pass behind early
Turn S to run along with it
why: Treat a moving cell like a ship crossing at 18 kn: you cannot outpace it, so slow down, let it cross, then pass behind it.
ref: Thunderstorms — dodging a cell offshore

fig.note: Radar, 2300 · cell moving S at 18 kn

q: Your crew want to motor east at 7 kn to outrun this squall line. When does it reach you if you do?
a: In about 50 min
o: In about 28 min
In about 36 min
In about 2 h 09 min
why: It closes at 25 − 7 = 18 kn: 15 M takes 50 min instead of 36. You gain 14 minutes — use them to reef, not to run.
ref: Thunderstorms — the squall line

fig.title: Radar, 1500
lines: Squall line 15 M W of you
Gusts in it forecast to 45 kn

q: Lightning struck the water close aboard in the night, and now the steering compass and the GPS disagree. What do you do?
a: Steer by GPS; check and swing the compass later
o: Trust the compass — the GPS has been hit
Apply the 19° as deviation, as usual
Apply the 19° as a change of variation
why: A near strike can magnetise steel aboard and shift the deviation: steer by GPS, check by the sun or a transit, and have it swung.
ref: Thunderstorms — after a near strike

fig.title: After the lightning, 0300
lines: GPS COG as a compass course: 128°C

q: You are on watch at 0200, 120 M offshore under a towering cloud, and you see this. What does it tell you?
a: St Elmo's fire — lightning may strike soon
o: A masthead light shorting — check the wiring
Phosphorescence — plankton in the spray
The tricolour reflected in the rain
why: St Elmo's fire is a glow discharge in a strong electric field: a strike is possible — keep the crew off the rig and away from metal.
ref: Thunderstorms — St Elmo's fire

fig.title: Night watch, 0200
lines: Towering cloud overhead, no rain yet
The hair on your arms stands up

q: You decide to run for this refuge rather than ride the gale out off a lee shore. When are you in, and with how much in hand?
a: In by about 2055 — 2 h 05 min in hand
o: In by about 1918 — 3 h 42 min in hand
In by about 2000 — 3 h 00 min in hand
In by about 2132 — 1 h 28 min in hand
why: Over the ground 7.5 − 1 = 6.5 kn: 45 ÷ 6.5 = 6.92 h = 6 h 55 min from 1400 — in at 2055, two hours before the gale.
ref: Heavy weather — a port of refuge

fig.title: 1400, gale warning
lines: You make 7.5 kn; stream 1 kn against
Lee shore 50 M E of you

q: You must ride out this gale at sea, with no port open to you. Which tactic can you keep up for the whole gale?
a: Heave to — about 42 M of drift
o: Run off with a drogue — about 105 M
Run off with a drogue — about 9 M
Heave to — about 21 M of drift
why: 30 h × 1.4 kn = 42 M hove-to, inside your 80 M; running at 3.5 kn needs 105 M — more sea room than you have.
ref: Heavy weather — tactics and sea room

fig.title: SW gale 9, for 30 h
lines: Lee shore: 80 M to the NE
Running with a drogue: about 3.5 kn
No port you can enter in it

q: You get this warning 140 M offshore, and your crew want to beat for the nearest port. What do you do?
a: Prepare the boat and ride it out at sea
o: Beat for the port before the gale arrives
Motor hard for the port, in by tomorrow
Run back downwind to the coast you left
why: 90 M to windward is 18 h or more — the gale will catch you on the way, and the coast astern becomes a lee shore. Use the sea room.
ref: Heavy weather — sea room or a port

fig.title: Gale warning, 1200
lines: Coast you left: 140 M NE — a lee shore
Open, deep water all round you

q: You hove-to through the night's gale and now want to resume your course to windward. When do you go?
a: In a few hours — the sea lags the wind
o: Now — the wind is down to force 5
Now — a big sea drops as fast as the wind
In two days — a sea never eases sooner
why: The old sea takes many hours to go down after the wind eases: beating into a steep 5 m sea now risks gear and crew for little gain.
ref: Heavy weather — after the gale

fig.title: Morning after the gale
lines: 0800: NW 5, sea still 5 m and steep

q: You are 110 M offshore at night, and no warning has come in yet. What does your barometer tell you to prepare for?
a: A storm — force 10 is likely
o: A gale — force 8 at most
A near gale — one more reef
Nothing until a warning comes
why: 11 hPa in 3 h is past the 10 hPa rule of thumb: a storm is likely. Prepare now — a warning can lag what the barometer shows.
ref: Barometer — the rate of fall and a storm

fig.title: Barometer log
lines: Rule of thumb, fall in 3 h:
10 hPa or more — a storm likely

q: You are driving your motor yacht towards a low, and the barometer has dropped fast. What is the real tendency, without your own run?
a: 3.0 hPa — falling
o: 5.4 hPa — falling quickly
7.8 hPa — falling very rapidly
1.4 hPa — falling slowly
why: 48 M at 16 kn across 4 hPa per 80 M accounts for 2.4 hPa: 5.4 − 2.4 = 3.0 hPa in 3 h — 'falling', not 'falling quickly'.
ref: Barometer — the tendency on a moving yacht

fig.title: Motor yacht, last 3 h
lines: Isobars: 4 hPa per 80 M on your track
